title: Honey Badgers: Small but Brave
summary: How the honey badger, a small member of the weasel family that lives in Africa, Asia, and Saudi Arabia, uses its loose skin, strong claws, venom resistance, and bad smell to survive and raid beehives.
poll: Being brave matters more than being big.

versions.title: Honey Badgers: Small but Brave
versions.text:
This is a honey badger. It is not big. But it is very brave.

It lives in hot, dry lands. It lives in Africa. It lives in parts of Asia, too. Some live in Saudi Arabia.

It has black fur. Its back is gray or white. It is as big as a small dog.

Its skin is thick. It is loose, too. A big cat may bite it. But it can twist. Then it can bite back!

It has long claws. It digs fast. It digs a hole to sleep in. The hole is a burrow.

It eats lots of things. It eats bugs and mice. It eats snakes, too. Some snakes have venom. Their bite can kill. But the badger can live. It may sleep a while. Then it wakes up!

It likes to raid bee hives. It eats the young bees. It eats the sweet food the bees make. That is how it got its name.

Is it scared? Then it makes a bad smell. Most beasts leave it be.

It is small. But it is brave and tough.

versions.title: Honey Badgers: Small but Brave

Meet the honey badger. It is not big. But it may be one of the most brave.

Honey badgers live in hot, dry places. They live in Africa and in parts of Asia. Some live in Saudi Arabia, too.

A honey badger has black fur on its legs and belly. Its back has a wide gray or white stripe. It is about the size of a small dog.

Its skin is very thick. It is loose, too. A lion may grab it. But the badger can twist in its skin. Then it can turn and bite back!

It has long, strong claws. It can dig very fast. It digs a hole to rest in. This hole is called a burrow.

Honey badgers eat many things. They eat bugs, mice, birds, and fruit. They eat snakes, too. Some snakes have venom. Their bite can kill most small animals. But a honey badger can live through it. It may sleep for a while. Then it wakes up and goes on!

Honey badgers love to raid bee hives. They eat the young bees and the honey. That is how they got their name.

Is a honey badger scared? Then it can make a bad smell. Most beasts leave it alone.

versions.title: Honey Badgers: Small but Brave
versions.text:
The honey badger is not a large animal. But many people say it is one of the bravest animals in the world.

Honey badgers live in warm, dry places. They are found in much of Africa and in parts of Asia. Some even live in the deserts and hills of Saudi Arabia.

A honey badger has black fur on its legs and belly. A wide gray or white stripe runs down its back. It is about the size of a small dog.

Its skin is very thick and loose. A lion may grab it. But the badger can twist around in its skin. Then it can turn and bite back!

It has long, strong claws on its front feet. It uses them to dig very fast. It digs a hole in the ground to rest in. This hole is called a burrow.

Honey badgers eat almost anything. They eat bugs, mice, birds, and fruit. They even eat snakes. Some snakes have venom, a poison that can kill most small animals. But a bitten honey badger can often live. It may sleep for a few hours. Then it wakes up and walks away!

They also love to break into bee hives. They eat the young bees and the honey. That is how they got their name.

When it is scared, a honey badger can make a very bad smell. Most animals leave it alone.

versions.title: Honey Badgers: Small but Brave
versions.text:
The honey badger is only about as big as a small dog. Yet many people call it one of the bravest animals on Earth.

Honey badgers are found across much of Africa and in parts of western and southern Asia. They live in many kinds of places, from grassland to rocky hills. Some live in the deserts and mountains of Saudi Arabia.

A honey badger is easy to spot. Its legs and belly are covered in black fur. A wide gray or white stripe runs along its back, from its head to its tail.

Its skin is one of its best tools. It is thick and very loose. If a lion or a leopard grabs it, the badger can twist around inside its own skin. Then it can turn and bite its attacker!

It also has long, curved claws on its front feet. It uses them to dig very quickly. Most days, it rests in a burrow. This is a hole it digs in the ground.

Honey badgers eat almost anything they can find. They hunt insects, scorpions, mice, birds, and lizards. They also eat fruit and roots. They even catch snakes. Some snakes have venom, a poison that can kill most small animals. But a bitten honey badger often lives. It may sleep for a few hours. Then it wakes up and walks away.

Honey badgers also break into bee hives to eat the young bees and the honey. That is how they got their name.

When it feels scared, a honey badger can give off a terrible smell. Most other animals decide to leave it alone.

versions.title: Honey Badgers: Small but Fearless
versions.text:
The honey badger is only about as big as a medium-sized dog. Yet many people call it one of the most fearless animals on Earth. It has been seen chasing young lions away from food, and it will even stand up to a pack of hyenas.

Honey badgers belong to the weasel family. They live in much of Africa and in parts of western and southern Asia, including the deserts and mountains of Saudi Arabia. Most adults weigh between six and fourteen kilograms. Their legs and belly are black, and a wide gray or white stripe runs along the back.

Its body helps it stay safe. Its skin is thick and very loose. If a predator, such as a leopard, grabs it by the neck, the badger can twist around inside its skin and bite back. Its front claws are long and curved. It can dig a burrow in just a few minutes.

Honey badgers eat almost anything. They hunt bugs, scorpions, mice, birds, and lizards. They eat fruit and roots, too. They even catch deadly snakes. Scientists have found that honey badgers are partly resistant to some snake venom. A bitten badger may fall asleep for a few hours, but then it wakes up and keeps going.

The animal got its name because it raids beehives. It eats the honey, but it mostly wants the larvae. These are the soft young bees inside the comb. Its thick skin keeps out most of the stings.

Honey badgers are solitary, which means they usually live and hunt alone. A mother raises her cub by herself for more than a year. When an adult feels scared, it can make a terrible smell that makes most enemies back away.

versions.title: Honey Badgers: Small but Formidable
versions.text:
Although the honey badger is roughly the size of a medium-sized dog, it has earned a reputation as one of the most formidable animals in the wild. Wildlife researchers have observed honey badgers chasing young lions away from a meal and confronting entire packs of hyenas, behavior that seems surprising for a creature that weighs so little.

Honey badgers belong to the weasel family, and their scientific name, Mellivora capensis, means "honey-eater from the Cape," a region of southern Africa. They are widespread across Africa and parts of western and southern Asia, including the deserts and rocky mountains of Saudi Arabia. Most adults weigh between six and fourteen kilograms. Their legs and underside are black, while a broad gray or silvery stripe extends along the back like a cape.

The honey badger's toughness comes from several physical adaptations, which are features that help an animal survive in its environment. Its skin is unusually thick and loose, so if a predator such as a leopard seizes it by the neck, the badger can rotate inside its skin and bite its attacker. Its long, curved front claws allow it to excavate a burrow for shelter in just a few minutes.

Honey badgers are opportunistic feeders, meaning they eat whatever food they can find. They hunt insects, scorpions, rodents, birds, and lizards, and they also eat fruit and roots. They even capture venomous snakes, such as cobras. Scientists have discovered that honey badgers are partly resistant to certain snake venoms because of a tiny genetic change in their bodies. A bitten badger may collapse and sleep for a few hours, then recover and continue on its way.

The animal earned its common name because it raids beehives. It certainly eats honey, but it is primarily interested in the larvae, the soft young bees developing inside the comb, and its thick skin protects it from most of the stings.

Honey badgers are usually solitary, and a mother raises her cub alone for more than a year. When an adult feels threatened, a gland near its tail can release a powerful odor that helps deter most enemies, who often decide that attacking such a stubborn animal is not worth the risk.

HIGH.prompt: Choose the honey badger adaptation you think is most important for its survival. Explain your choice using evidence from the article, and compare it with one other adaptation.
checklist: I named one adaptation and explained why it matters most.
I used specific evidence from the article.
I compared it with a second adaptation.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I think the honey badger's thick, loose skin is its most important adaptation, because it lets the animal twist inside its own hide and bite back even while a formidable predator like a leopard has it by the neck, turning a near-fatal attack into a chance to escape. This adaptation matters more than its partial resistance to snake venom, which only helps after a bite has already happened and can still leave the badger temporarily helpless for hours. The loose skin works proactively to prevent serious injury in the first place, which is especially valuable for such an opportunistic hunter that constantly tangles with dangerous prey and rivals. Its scent gland, which releases a powerful smell to deter enemies, is useful too, but it only scares attackers away rather than protecting the badger during an actual attack.
